Most of what's confusing about modern AI isn't the model itself — it's the plumbing built around it. Retrieval, tools, agents, evaluation: each one exists to patch a specific limit of the one before it. Once you see it as one connected chain instead of a pile of buzzwords, the whole field gets a lot less mysterious.

💡 New to this? You don't need to be an ML engineer — most of this is concepts and prompts, not code. Skim Foundations first if RAG or agents feel like jargon soup, and your first mental model won't be perfect, and that's completely normal.

The LLM the core loop
Quick disambiguation: an LLM answers one prompt from what it already knows; a RAG pipeline answers using your own retrieved documents; an agent takes multiple steps and actions toward a goal, using tools and memory. People use these terms loosely — naming the right one in your prompt gets you a much better first result.

See It Built, Start to Finish

One complete example — from messy raw data to a finished result — so you can see how the pieces fit together before we go section by section.
1 Start with your raw data

Say you have 40 support articles sitting in a folder, no structure beyond filenames:

FileTopicLengthLast updated
refunds-policy.mdBilling640 wordsMar 2026
shipping-domestic.mdShipping310 wordsJan 2026
account-deletion.mdAccount210 wordsNov 2025
api-rate-limits.mdAPI480 wordsJun 2026
password-reset.mdAccount150 wordsFeb 2026
2 Write one plain-English prompt

You don't describe code — you describe what you want the system to do, in your own words:

Prompt: "Chunk these articles semantically, embed them, and build a retrieval step that answers only from the top-3 reranked chunks. If nothing relevant is found, say so — don't guess."
3 What comes back

An illustrative sketch of the result — this is what a grounded answer actually looks like assembled together:

40 docs indexed
8 chunks retrieved
3 used after rerank
🔍 Retrieval — semantic chunks, hybrid search
Query: "how long do refunds take?"
Answer
"Based on refunds-policy.md, domestic refunds take 5–7 business days."
4 Why these choices
  • Semantic chunking — support articles vary wildly in length, so fixed-size chunks would split answers mid-sentence.
  • Hybrid search + reranking — the first vector pass over-retrieves; reranking filters down to what's actually relevant.
  • Top-3 after rerank — enough context to answer fully without diluting the model with near-duplicate chunks.
  • Explicit "say so if not found" — the single instruction that prevents most hallucination in a RAG pipeline.
That's the whole loop: documents → plain-English prompt → grounded result → one look at whether it matches what you actually needed. Everything below breaks each of those steps down further, level by level.

🪜 Step by step

From Blank Page to Working System

Everything above is the menu. This is the order you actually work through it in, with a prompt for each step.
  1. Step 1 of 7Gather your data or define the task. Docs to retrieve from, an API to call, or just a clearly written goal — read files in place or work from what you describe.
  2. Step 2 of 7Pick your depth. Foundations, Intermediate, or Expert — match it to how much autonomy the task actually needs.
  3. Step 3 of 7Pick the shape. A single grounded answer (RAG), an action-taker (agent), or a team of them (multi-agent) — see the Production / Scale section for when it needs to be reliable, not just clever.
  4. Step 4 of 7Pick your priority. One-shot, Grounded, Iterative, or Production — this decides which tradeoffs are worth making.
  5. Step 5 of 7Write one combined prompt. Stack the choices above into a single request rather than a vague one. See the example below.
  6. Step 6 of 7Review and refine one thing at a time. Don't ask for five changes in one message — fix retrieval, then tool errors, then guardrails. Big multi-part edits are where quality drops.
  7. Step 7 of 7Evaluate before you trust it. Run the Review Checklist and spot-check real outputs against source data before calling it done.
Prompt: "Build a RAG-backed assistant over {docs}: semantic chunking, hybrid retrieval, rerank to top-3, explicit \"not found\" fallback. Depth: Intermediate. Priority: accuracy over cost."
Prompt: "Harden this system for production: tracing on every step, a fallback for tool or API failure, a held-out eval run before each change, and guardrails treating retrieved content as untrusted."
Rule of thumb: name the depth, the shape, and the priority explicitly in the prompt. Those three words do more work than any amount of extra styling detail.
⚠️ Common mistakes
  • Asking for everything in one prompt. Chunking strategy, reranking, tool schema, and guardrails all at once tends to produce a worse result than four smaller requests in sequence.
  • Giving an agent no stop condition. "Keep trying until it works" with no retry limit is how a single bad tool call turns into a runaway loop and a runaway bill.
  • Not naming the depth. "Build me an agent" gives no signal on how much autonomy belongs in the system — say Foundations, Intermediate, or Expert explicitly.
  • Treating a public benchmark as your eval. If your task resembles the benchmark's training data, a high score may just reflect memorization, not real capability.
  • Trusting the first result without a spot-check. Always verify a few outputs against source data before sharing — see the Review Checklist.
🎨 Visual polish

Diagram & Notation Conventions

Three low-risk conventions for diagramming these systems — pick one, stay consistent, instead of inventing new shapes per diagram.

Trust Boundary ✓ If unsure

Shade any box receiving untrusted content (retrieved docs, tool output, user input) — makes injection surfaces visible in the diagram itself.

Pipeline Notation

Rounded boxes = model calls, diamonds = retrieval/lookup steps, dashed arrows = optional/conditional paths.

Cost / Latency Labels

Label each step with approximate token cost or call count — makes "why is this slow/expensive" visible on the page.

92%Retrieval confidence — Grounded
Pick a palette above to preview it here.
Prompt: "Redraw this pipeline with rounded boxes for model calls, diamonds for retrieval steps, and shade any box that receives untrusted external content."
🎨 Visual polish

Explaining These Systems Clearly

The difference between notes that inform and notes that just look thorough.

Lead with the failure mode

State what breaks and why before the mechanism — that's what the reader actually came for.

One idea per callout

If you can't summarize the point in one sentence, it's two callouts, not one.

One technique per card

Resist cramming three techniques into one card — split it into separate reference entries instead.

Bold sparingly

Bold only the one term or number that matters. If everything is emphasized, nothing is.

Don't rely on color alone

Pair every pass/fail eval badge with an icon or label too (●Passed, ▲Regressed, ✕Failed) — around 1 in 12 men have some form of color blindness.

Contrast & size

Aim for at least 4.5:1 text contrast, and keep body text no smaller than 14px — diagrams get projected and shrunk more than you'd expect.

Prompt: "Make sure every pass/fail badge pairs a color with an icon or text label, not color alone. Keep body text at least 14px and headline numbers high-contrast against the background."

📖 Glossary

Terms & Prompts Used in This Guide

Two lists: the short-form codes and abbreviations, and every copy-ready prompt from this guide gathered in one place.
📟 Codes & Abbreviations

Token

The subword unit an LLM actually reads and writes — never whole letters or words.

Embedding

A vector representation of meaning — distance and direction encode relationships.

Context window

How much text a model can attend to at once — effective recall is often shorter than the advertised size.

RAG

Retrieval-augmented generation — grounding answers in your own retrieved documents.

Reranker

A cross-encoder model that re-scores retrieved chunks for relevance after an initial fast retrieval pass.

ReAct

Interleaved Thought → Action → Observation pattern for agent reasoning and tool use.

LoRA / QLoRA

Lightweight fine-tuning methods that adapt a model without retraining all its weights.

Agent

A model looping through plan → act → observe steps, using tools and memory toward a goal.

Multi-agent orchestration

Specialized agents (planner, worker, critic) handing off tasks via a defined schema.

LLM-as-judge

Using a model to grade outputs at scale — watch for self-preference and position bias.

Guardrail

A check that constrains model input or output — e.g. treating retrieved content as untrusted.

Quantization

Compressing a model (GGUF/AWQ/GPTQ) to run cheaper or faster, with uneven capability tradeoffs.

Prompt caching

Providers charge less for repeated context prefixes — prompt structure affects cost.

Hallucination

A confident, fabricated answer — reduced but not eliminated by retrieval.

RLHF / DPO

Alignment methods using human preference — also the mechanical root of sycophancy.

✅ Quality gate

Before You Hit Send: Review Checklist

Click to check off — nothing here is saved, it just helps you go through the list once before sharing.
  • Retrieved context spot-checked against source
  • Tool descriptions don't overlap in purpose
  • Agent has an explicit stop condition
  • Eval set is held-out, not benchmark-contaminated
  • Retrieved / tool content treated as untrusted input
  • Tested with an adversarial or edge-case prompt
  • No placeholder text, dummy links, or "lorem ipsum" left in
Self-critique prompt — paste this back before shipping: "Review this system critically: check for hallucination risk, prompt injection surfaces, and unclear failure modes. Suggest 3 specific improvements."
📤 Last mile

Where These Systems Live

Where a pipeline or agent lives after you build it changes what you should ask for.

Keep as living notes

Best default for a personal reference like this one — easy to keep extending as the field moves.

Export a pipeline to a repo

Once a RAG/agent design is validated, it belongs in version control with tests — not just a prompt in a chat window.

Export a diagram to slides

For a team readout, ask for "one slide per pipeline stage, with the trust-boundary shading kept."

Wire into a real API

Once validated in a notebook or chat, the pipeline moves behind an endpoint with its own logging and rate limits.

Static snapshot for review

Fine for a one-off design review or handoff document — but it flattens everything, so use it only for a snapshot, never as your working copy.

Keep one source of truth

Treat the working notes/pipeline as the master copy, and generate flattened exports (slides, docs) from it only when a specific audience needs a static version.

🛠 When It Goes Wrong

Quick Fixes for Bad Generations

You're staring at a broken or wrong result on screen. Here's what to do immediately, before you start over from scratch.

Answers ignore retrieved content

Say explicitly: "answer only using the provided context, quote the exact source chunk you used." Vague instructions invite the model to fall back on its own memory.

Agent loops forever

Add a hard cap: "stop and ask for clarification after 3 consecutive failed tool calls." Missing stop conditions are the most common cause of runaway loops.

Retrieval returns nothing useful

Check chunking first, not the model — oversized or misaligned chunks are the single most common cause of poor retrieval.

Tool called with wrong arguments

Tighten the tool description and remove overlap with any similarly-named tool — ambiguous schemas are the leading cause of wrong-tool selection.

Eval scores look too good

Check for benchmark contamination or an eval set too close to training data — swap in a genuinely held-out set.

Output breaks structured parsing

If strict JSON schema is degrading answer quality, let the model reason freely first, then extract structure afterward.

Multi-agent handoff drops context

Define a strict handoff schema (task, context, tool-access) instead of free-form text between agents — ambiguous handoffs are where context gets lost.

Prompt only partly followed

You likely asked for too much in one message. Split it: get retrieval right first, then tool calls, then guardrails, then polish — one request per message.

General habit that fixes most of the above: after 2–3 failed patch attempts on the same issue, stop patching. Ask for a clean regeneration with a more specific prompt instead — small incremental fixes on a shaky base tend to compound the problem rather than solve it.
Before you trust an answer: spot-check at least two or three claims against the source yourself. AI-generated systems are convenient, not infallible — a five-second manual check catches most "confidently wrong" outputs.
